topics.title: Need for entrepreneurship and the entrepreneurial process

learn.hook: India needs crores of new jobs every decade. Government offices and big companies alone cannot create them; entrepreneurs can.
points: Need for entrepreneurship in economic development: it raises production and GDP; encourages capital formation by mobilising savings; generates employment for the entrepreneur and others; creates business opportunities for suppliers and other firms; improves economic efficiency through innovation; increases the scope of economic activities; benefits local communities; and fosters a spirit of exploration and adventure.

There is no single fixed list of stages; one common way to describe the journey of starting a venture is: (1) identify a business opportunity or idea; (2) evaluate it through feasibility study and market research; (3) prepare a business plan; (4) mobilise resources such as finance, people, technology and premises; (5) launch the enterprise and manage it; (6) grow and expand.
Ideas often come from problems people face, changes in technology, new trends and gaps in existing markets.
A business plan describes the product, target market, competitors, operations, team and financial projections; it guides the founder and convinces investors and lenders.
In the CBSE syllabus, the process of entrepreneurship development is studied mainly through the Startup India scheme and the ways to fund start-ups (next topic).

example.q: Rahul notices that people in his town have no affordable bicycle repair service. He surveys demand, writes a plan, borrows money, opens a shop and later opens two more. Map his steps to the process.
steps: Notices the gap: identify opportunity.
Surveys demand: evaluate the idea.
Writes a plan: business plan.
Borrows money and sets up: mobilise resources and launch.
Opens two more: growth.
example.answer: Opportunity → evaluation → business plan → resources → launch → growth.

learn.reallife: Incubation centres at IITs, IIMs and many universities help students move from idea to business plan to launch.

topics.title: Startup India and ways to fund start-ups

learn.hook: In 2016 India launched Startup India. Today the country has one of the largest startup ecosystems in the world. How do these ventures get their first rupee?
points: Startup India was launched by the Government of India on 16 January 2016 to build a strong ecosystem for innovation and start-ups, drive economic growth and create jobs.

Its action plan focuses on three areas: simplification and handholding (easier compliance, self-certification, a single online hub); funding support and incentives (a Fund of Funds, credit guarantees, tax benefits for recognised start-ups); and industry-academia partnership and incubation (incubators, research parks, innovation challenges).

Bootstrapping: funding the venture with the founder's own savings and early revenues, keeping costs low. Crowdfunding: raising small amounts from a large number of people, usually through online platforms.

Angel investment: wealthy individuals invest their own money in early-stage start-ups in exchange for equity, often adding mentoring. Venture capital: professionally managed funds invest in high-growth start-ups for equity, along with guidance, usually at a later stage than angels.

Business incubators and accelerators: incubators nurture very early-stage ideas with space, mentoring and networks over a longer period; accelerators run short, intensive programmes to speed up the growth of existing start-ups. Microfinance and NBFCs: small loans to entrepreneurs who lack access to regular banking.

example.q: Arrange a typical funding journey of a tech start-up: venture capital, bootstrapping, angel investment.
steps: The founder first uses own savings: bootstrapping.
Then an individual investor puts in early money: angel investment.
Later a professional fund invests for growth: venture capital.
example.answer: Bootstrapping → angel investment → venture capital.

learn.reallife: Startup India's portal lets founders apply for recognition online, and many state governments run their own startup policies and incubators.

learn.hook: Your brand name, your app's code, your invention and even the region your tea comes from can all be protected by law. Ideas are property too.
points: Intellectual property refers to creations of the mind: inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names and images used in business. Intellectual property rights (IPR) are legal rights that protect these creations and give the creator exclusive rights to use them for a period.

Copyright: protects literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, cinematograph films, sound recordings and computer software. Trademark: a word, name, symbol, logo or design that distinguishes the goods or services of one firm from others (registration is valid for 10 years and renewable).

Patent: an exclusive right granted for an invention that is new, involves an inventive step and is capable of industrial application; in India, a patent lasts 20 years. Design: protects the new or original shape, configuration, pattern or ornamentation applied to an article (its visual appearance).

Geographical indication (GI): identifies goods as originating from a specific place, where a quality or reputation is linked to that origin, e.g. Darjeeling tea, Banarasi sarees, Kanchipuram silk. Plant variety: protects new plant varieties developed by breeders and farmers. Semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design: protects the layout of transistors and circuit elements on chips.
Why start-ups need IPR: to prevent copying of their innovation, build brand value, attract investors, earn through licensing, and gain a competitive edge.

example.q: A start-up (a) invents a new water-purifying filter, (b) names it 'PuriDrop' with a logo, and (c) writes the software for its app. Which IPR protects each?
steps: New invention with industrial application = patent.
Brand name and logo = trademark.
Computer software = copyright.
example.answer: (a) Patent, (b) trademark, (c) copyright.

learn.hook: Biscuits made in a factory near Pune reach a tiny shop in Arunachal. In between stands a quiet hero of trade: the wholesaler.
points: Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the boundaries of a nation. No customs duty or import duty is levied, since goods are produced and sold within the country. It is classified into wholesale trade and retail trade.
Wholesale trade means buying and selling goods in large quantities, usually from manufacturers, and selling them to retailers or other businesses (not to final consumers).

Services of wholesalers to manufacturers: facilitating large-scale production (by buying in bulk); bearing risk (of price fall, theft, spoilage); financial assistance (paying cash for goods, sometimes in advance); expert advice (on consumer preferences and market trends); help in marketing (distributing to many retailers); facilitating continuity of production; storage (warehousing goods until needed).

Services of wholesalers to retailers: availability of goods (ready stock from many producers); marketing support (advertising and promotion); grant of credit; specialised knowledge (about products and demand); risk sharing (retailers buy in small lots, so they carry less stock).

example.q: A wholesaler buys 10,000 packets of tea from a manufacturer each month, stores them and sells to 200 small shops on 15 days' credit. Name one service to the manufacturer and one to the retailers.
steps: Buying in bulk and storing goods helps the manufacturer produce on a large scale continuously.
Selling on 15 days' credit helps retailers: grant of credit.
example.answer: To manufacturer: facilitating large-scale production and storage; to retailers: grant of credit.

learn.hook: The corner kirana shop knows your family's favourite brand of atta, offers credit until the month-end and introduces new products. It is the final link to the consumer.
points: A retailer is a business enterprise that sells goods and services directly to final consumers for their personal, non-business use, usually in small quantities. Retailing is the last link in the chain of distribution.

Services to manufacturers and wholesalers: help in distribution (making goods available to scattered consumers); personal selling (explaining and persuading); enabling large-scale operations (so producers and wholesalers need not deal with each consumer); collecting market information (about tastes and preferences); help in promotion (displays and in-store promotion).

learn.hook: The vegetable vendor with a handcart, the weekly haat in a village, the man selling toys outside a railway station: retailers who come to you.
points: Itinerant retailers are traders who do not have a fixed place of business; they keep moving from place to place in search of customers. They deal in consumer goods of daily use, often of low value, and give time and place utility.
Peddlers and hawkers: carry goods on bicycles, handcarts, cycle-rickshaws or on their heads, and sell from place to place at the doorstep of customers, e.g. vegetables, fruits, snacks, toys.
Market traders: open shops at different places on fixed days or dates, e.g. weekly markets (haats) on Mondays in one place and Thursdays in another.

Street traders (pavement vendors): sell at places with huge floating population, such as near railway stations, bus stands and busy streets; they sell common-use items like stationery, eatables, newspapers and readymade garments.

Cheap jacks: have independent shops of a temporary nature in a business locality; they keep changing their location depending on the potential of the place, and deal in consumer items and repairs (e.g. watches, shoes, buckets).

example.q: Ramu sets up a temporary stall near a new housing colony to repair shoes and sell buckets. After three months he shifts to another locality with better business. What type of itinerant retailer is he?

He shifts location according to business potential.
That describes a cheap jack.
example.answer: Cheap jack.

points: Fixed-shop retailers have permanent establishments to sell their goods; they have greater resources than itinerant retailers and offer more services like home delivery and credit.

learn.hook: Clothes on the first floor, electronics on the second, a café on the third, all under one roof. That is the departmental store.
points: A departmental store is a large establishment offering a wide variety of products, classified into well-defined departments, aimed at satisfying practically every need of the customer under one roof. Each department specialises in one line.

Features: large size, usually centrally located; provides facilities like restaurants, travel bureaus, rest rooms and parking under one roof; combines retailing with warehousing; buys directly from manufacturers; centralised purchasing and decentralised sales across departments; often organised as a company with a board.

Merits: attracts a large number of customers due to central location; convenience in buying (all needs under one roof); attractive services; economy of large-scale operations; promotion of sales through advertising and display.

Limitations: lack of personal attention to customers; high operating cost (rent, staff, services), so prices tend to be high; high possibility of losses due to high costs and changing demand; inconvenient location for buyers who need something urgently, since it is usually in the city centre.

topics.title: Chain stores (multiple shops) and comparison with departmental stores

learn.hook: The same shoe shop with the same look, same prices and same products in Pune, Patna and Puducherry: that is a chain store.
points: Chain stores or multiple shops are networks of retail shops owned and operated by manufacturers or intermediaries, located in different localities across the country, with similar appearance and dealing in standardised, branded products.

Features: located in fairly populous localities; manufacturing or purchasing is centralised at the head office; each shop is supervised by a branch manager; the head office controls policies; prices are fixed and all sales are on a cash basis; sales proceeds are deposited daily; dealing in a limited range of products.

Merits: economies of scale (central purchasing); elimination of middlemen; no bad debts (cash sales); transfer of goods from one branch to another; diffusion of risk (losses in one shop offset by profits in others); low cost of operation; flexibility (an unprofitable shop can be closed or shifted).

Limitations: limited selection of goods (only the firm's own range); lack of initiative (branch managers follow head office instructions); lack of personal touch; difficult to change products quickly when demand changes.

Departmental store vs chain store: one central location vs many localities near customers; wide variety of products vs limited range of a specific type; maximum services vs limited services; prices not uniform (discounts used to clear stock) vs uniform fixed prices; may give credit vs strictly cash; caters mostly to higher-income groups vs various income groups.

example.q: A shoe company has 400 shops across India. One shop in a small town keeps making losses. What can the company do, and which merits of chain stores does this show?
steps: It can close or shift the loss-making shop: flexibility.
Profits of the other shops cover this loss: diffusion of risk.
It can also move unsold stock to branches with higher demand.
example.answer: Close or shift the shop and move stock; shows flexibility, diffusion of risk and transfer of goods.

learn.hook: Long before apps, people in small towns ordered books, seeds and gadgets from catalogues and received them by post. That is mail order business.
points: Mail order houses are retail outlets that sell goods through mail. There is generally no direct personal contact between buyers and sellers.

Prospective customers are approached through advertisements in newspapers and magazines, circulars, catalogues, samples and price lists sent by post. Orders are received by mail, and goods are sent through the post office, often by VPP (value payable post), where the customer pays on delivery.
Suitable for: standardised and graded goods, which can be easily described; goods that can be transported easily at low cost; not suitable for perishable goods or goods requiring personal inspection.

Merits: limited capital requirement (no costly shop); elimination of middlemen; absence of bad debts (payment in advance or on delivery); wide reach (anywhere the post reaches); convenience (goods delivered at the doorstep).

Limitations: lack of personal contact; high promotion costs (advertising and catalogues); no after-sales services; no facility of credit; possibility of abuse (fraud by dishonest sellers); dependence on postal services.

example.q: A firm in Delhi sells standard-size calendars and diaries through catalogues sent by post and delivers them by VPP. Why are bad debts absent?
steps: Under VPP, the customer pays when the parcel is delivered.
The post office collects the money before handing over goods.
No goods are given on credit.
example.answer: Because payment is collected on delivery (VPP), so there is no credit and hence no bad debts.

learn.reallife: India Post's value payable post service made mail order business possible across small towns, and today's e-commerce is its digital descendant.

topics.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST): concept and structure

learn.hook: Before 2017, goods crossing state borders faced different taxes and long queues of trucks at check posts. GST changed this with 'One Nation, One Tax'.
points: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a comprehensive, destination-based indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services. It came into force on 1 July 2017 after the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016.

It replaced many central and state indirect taxes, such as central excise duty, service tax, VAT, central sales tax, entry tax, octroi and luxury tax. Destination-based means the tax revenue goes to the state where goods or services are consumed.

Intra-state supply (within the same state): Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) are levied, shared equally; in Union Territories without their own legislature, UTGST replaces SGST. Example: at 18%, it is CGST 9% + SGST 9%.
Inter-state supply (from one state to another) and imports: Integrated GST (IGST) is levied by the Centre, and later shared with the destination state. Example: at 18%, IGST is 18%.
The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister and including state finance ministers, recommends GST rates, exemptions and rules.

example.q: A trader in Jaipur sells goods worth ₹50,000 at 18% GST (a) to a buyer in Jodhpur and (b) to a buyer in Pune. What taxes apply in each case?
steps: (a) Jaipur to Jodhpur is within Rajasthan: intra-state.
(b) Jaipur to Pune is from Rajasthan to Maharashtra: inter-state.

learn.reallife: After GST, many state-border check posts were removed, cutting the time trucks spend waiting on highways.

topics.title: Input tax credit, GSTN, composition scheme and chambers of commerce

learn.hook: Before GST, a shopkeeper often paid tax on tax: the tax already included in his purchase price was taxed again when he sold. Input tax credit fixed this.
points: Input tax credit (ITC): a registered business can deduct the GST it has already paid on purchases (input tax) from the GST it collects on sales (output tax), and pays only the difference. This removes the cascading effect (tax on tax).
GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) is the IT backbone of GST: it provides the online portal for registration, filing returns and paying tax for taxpayers, the Centre and states.

Registration: businesses whose aggregate turnover crosses a prescribed threshold must register. At present the threshold is ₹40 lakh a year for most suppliers of goods and ₹20 lakh for service providers, with lower limits in some special-category states; the government can revise it.

Composition scheme: an optional, simpler scheme for small taxpayers (turnover up to ₹1.5 crore for most traders and manufacturers), who pay tax at a low fixed rate on their turnover with fewer returns; they cannot claim input tax credit and cannot charge GST to their customers on their bills.

Chambers of commerce and industry, such as FICCI, CII and ASSOCHAM, promote internal trade by working with government on transportation and inter-state movement, harmonisation of taxes and levies, marketing of agro-products, weights and measures and prevention of duplicate brands, promoting sound infrastructure, and simplifying labour laws.

example.q: A manufacturer sells goods to a retailer for ₹10,000 + 18% GST. The retailer sells them for ₹15,000 + 18% GST. How much GST does the retailer pay to the government after input tax credit?
steps: Input tax (paid on purchase) = 18% of 10,000 = ₹1,800.
Output tax (collected on sale) = 18% of 15,000 = ₹2,700.
Net GST payable = 2,700 − 1,800 = ₹900.
This equals 18% of the value added (₹5,000).

learn.reallife: Every month lakhs of businesses file their GST returns online on the GST portal run by GSTN.

learn.hook: Indian software runs banks in London, Gulf oil fuels Indian cars, and Japanese technology makes Indian metro coaches. No country is an island in business.
points: International business refers to manufacturing and trade beyond national boundaries. It includes not only cross-border trade in goods and services, but also the movement of capital, personnel, technology and intellectual property (patents, trademarks, know-how and copyrights).

International trade means exports and imports of goods and services. International business is wider: it covers trade plus foreign investment, licensing, franchising and other forms of cross-border operations.

Main reason: countries cannot produce everything equally well or cheaply, because of unequal distribution of natural resources (e.g. oil in the Gulf, iron ore in some countries) and differences in labour productivity and production costs.
So each country specialises in what it can produce more efficiently and trades for the rest. This specialisation benefits all trading nations.

example.q: India imports crude oil but exports IT services. Explain why, using the reasons for international business.
steps: India does not have enough crude oil reserves: unequal distribution of natural resources.
India has a large pool of skilled, cost-effective IT professionals: differences in labour productivity and costs.
So India specialises in IT services and trades for oil.
example.answer: Due to unequal natural resources and differences in labour productivity and costs, India specialises in IT and imports oil.

learn.reallife: Indian generic medicines are exported to many countries because India can produce them at lower cost: specialisation in action.

topics.title: Domestic vs international business; scope of international business

learn.hook: Selling sarees in Jaipur and selling sarees in Japan both involve sarees, but the currency, laws, customers and risks are completely different.
points: Differences between domestic and international business: nationality of buyers and sellers (same vs different countries); nationality of other stakeholders (employees, suppliers, investors); mobility of factors of production (free within a country, restricted across countries); customer heterogeneity (different tastes, languages, cultures); differences in business systems and practices; political systems and risks; business regulations and policies (tariffs, quotas, standards); currency (one currency vs different currencies and exchange-rate changes).

Scope: merchandise exports and imports (tangible goods); service exports and imports, also called invisible trade (tourism and travel, transportation, business services such as banking, insurance, software).

topics.title: Modes of entry: exporting/importing and contract manufacturing

learn.hook: A firm can enter a foreign market by just shipping goods there, or by getting a local factory to make its products. These are the two simplest doors to global business.
points: Exporting means sending goods and services from the home country to a foreign country; importing means buying them from abroad. Direct exporting/importing: the firm itself approaches overseas buyers or suppliers and handles all formalities. Indirect: the firm works through intermediaries such as export houses or buying offices of foreign customers.
Merits of exporting/importing: the easiest way to enter international markets; less involvement and less investment (no need to set up units abroad); less risk compared with other modes.

Limitations: added costs of packaging, transportation and insurance make goods costlier abroad; not possible where the importing country has restrictions; exporters operate from home and have little direct contact with foreign markets.

Contract manufacturing (outsourcing): a firm enters into a contract with local manufacturers in foreign countries to produce certain components or goods as per its specifications. Merits: large-scale production without investing in facilities; little investment risk; cost advantage (local labour and materials); local producers get business.

Limitations of contract manufacturing: local firms may not follow quality standards; the local manufacturer loses control over the manufacturing process, since goods are made strictly as per the contract; the local firm cannot sell the goods freely and must sell to the international firm at predetermined prices.

example.q: A European clothing brand gets an Indian factory in Tiruppur to make T-shirts with its designs and labels, and buys all of them at an agreed price. Which mode of entry is this, and one limitation for the Indian factory?
steps: Production by a local firm as per the foreign firm's specifications = contract manufacturing.
The Indian factory must sell to the brand at predetermined prices and cannot sell the T-shirts freely.
example.answer: Contract manufacturing; the local firm cannot sell freely and gets predetermined prices.

learn.reallife: Many global brands get their garments, phones and toys made by contract manufacturers in India.

topics.title: Modes of entry: licensing, franchising, joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries

learn.hook: A burger chain's outlet in Delhi, a car plant owned jointly by Indian and foreign firms, and a foreign company's 100%-owned Indian unit: three deeper ways to go global.
points: Licensing: a firm (licensor) permits a foreign firm (licensee) to use its patents, trademarks, copyrights or technical know-how for a fee called royalty. Franchising is similar but is generally used for services; the franchiser gives a business model and exercises stricter control over the franchisee. Merits: less expensive and low risk for the licensor (licensee invests); licensor does not bear losses; low risk of government takeover as local owners run the business; licensee's local knowledge helps. Limitations: licensee may later become a competitor; trade secrets may leak; conflicts over accounts, royalty and quality.

Joint venture (JV): a firm jointly owned by two or more independent firms. It can be formed when a foreign firm buys an interest in a local firm, a local firm buys an interest in a foreign firm, or both jointly form a new enterprise. Merits: less financial burden for the foreign firm; large projects become possible; benefit of the local partner's knowledge of markets, culture and politics; risks are shared. Limitations: technology and trade secrets may be revealed to the partner; dual ownership can cause conflicts.

Wholly owned subsidiary (WOS): the parent company acquires full control (100% equity) over a foreign company, either by setting up a new firm (greenfield venture) or by acquiring an established firm. Merits: full control over operations; no need to share technology or trade secrets. Limitations: 100% investment, so not suitable for small and medium firms; the parent bears all losses; some countries are averse to full foreign ownership, raising political risk.
Comparing modes: exporting and licensing need the least investment abroad; a joint venture needs more; a wholly owned subsidiary needs the most investment and gives the most control.

example.q: A foreign pizza brand lets an Indian company run outlets under its name, menu and systems, and checks quality strictly in return for fees. Which mode is this, and how does it differ from licensing?
steps: Use of brand plus a full business system in services, with strict control = franchising.
Licensing is mainly for production and marketing of goods using patents or know-how, with less control.
Franchising is mainly for services, with stricter control by the franchiser.
example.answer: Franchising; it applies to services with stricter control, while licensing applies to goods.

topics.title: Export procedure (I): from enquiry to production

learn.hook: A buyer in Dubai emails an Indian carpet maker in Bhadohi asking for prices. Seventeen steps later, the carpets are on a ship and the money is in the bank.
points: Step 1, receipt of enquiry and sending quotations: the importer asks about prices, quality and terms; the exporter replies with a quotation, often in the form of a proforma invoice (giving details of quality, grade, size, weight, price and terms of export).
Step 2, receipt of order or indent: if the importer accepts, he places an order or indent describing the goods, price, quantity, packing and delivery terms.

Step 3, assessing the importer's creditworthiness and securing a guarantee for payment: the exporter usually asks for a letter of credit, a guarantee issued by the importer's bank that it will honour payment up to a certain amount.

Step 4, obtaining an export licence: the exporter must get an Importer Exporter Code (IEC) number from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), and register with the appropriate Export Promotion Council (getting a Registration-cum-Membership Certificate, RCMC); registration with the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) protects against payment risks.
Step 5, obtaining pre-shipment finance from a bank to buy raw materials, process and pack goods; Step 6, production or procurement of goods as per the importer's specifications.

example.q: Put these early export steps in order: obtain IEC number, receive order, send proforma invoice, get letter of credit.
steps: First reply to the enquiry with a proforma invoice (quotation).
Then receive the order or indent.
Then secure payment guarantee: letter of credit.
Then obtain the export licence, including the IEC number.
example.answer: Send proforma invoice → receive order → get letter of credit → obtain IEC number.

learn.reallife: The DGFT issues IEC numbers online; without one, an Indian business cannot legally export or import.

topics.title: Export procedure (II): from inspection to payment

learn.hook: The carpets are ready. Now come inspection, customs, the ship's receipt, the bill of lading and finally the payment.
points: Step 7, shipment inspection: for certain goods, inspection by the Export Inspection Agency (EIA) or another authorised body is compulsory, and a certificate of inspection is issued. Step 8, excise clearance: the book lists this step, in which the exporter applies to the excise authorities for clearance of excise duty on the goods; such duty on exports was generally exempted or refunded, and since 2017 GST has replaced central excise on most goods, with exports treated as zero-rated. Step 9, obtaining a certificate of origin, which shows the country where goods are made, so the importer may claim tariff concessions.

Step 10, reservation of shipping space: the exporter applies to the shipping company; it issues a shipping order, an instruction to the captain of the ship to receive the specified goods on board. Step 11, packing and forwarding: goods are properly packed and marked and sent to the port. Step 12, insurance of goods against risks at sea.

Step 13, customs clearance: the exporter prepares a shipping bill, the main document on the basis of which customs gives permission to export. Step 14, obtaining mate's receipt: after loading, the captain (mate) of the ship issues a mate's receipt to the exporter, acknowledging receipt of the cargo on board.

Step 15, payment of freight and issue of bill of lading: on paying freight, the shipping company issues a bill of lading, which is evidence that it has accepted the goods for carriage and is a document of title (an airway bill is used for air cargo). Step 16, preparation of invoice, stating quantity and the amount payable.

Step 17, securing payment: the exporter sends the shipping documents through his bank to the importer's bank, along with a bill of exchange. Under a sight draft, documents are released on payment (D/P); under a usance draft, documents are released on acceptance of the bill (D/A), and payment is made later.

learn.hook: A Ludhiana firm wants machines from Germany. It must find a supplier, get permission, arrange foreign currency, pay and clear customs before the machines reach its factory.
points: Step 1, trade enquiry: the importer collects information about exporters and their terms, and asks for quotations (often receiving a proforma invoice). Step 2, procurement of import licence: the importer checks the EXIM policy to see if a licence is needed, and must have an IEC number from the DGFT.

Step 3, obtaining foreign exchange: the importer applies to a bank authorised by the RBI for foreign exchange, as per foreign exchange regulations. Step 4, placing order or indent with the exporter. Step 5, obtaining a letter of credit from his bank in favour of the exporter, if agreed.

Step 6, arranging finance to pay for the goods on arrival. Step 7, receipt of shipment advice from the exporter, giving details such as invoice number, bill of lading number, name of vessel, port and date of shipment.

Step 8, retirement of import documents: the importer pays (sight draft) or accepts the bill of exchange (usance draft) to get the shipping documents, such as the bill of lading, from the bank. Step 9, arrival of goods at the port.

Step 10, customs clearance and release of goods: the importer gets a delivery order from the shipping company, pays the dock dues (getting a port trust dues receipt), fills in a bill of entry (giving details of goods for customs and assessment of import duty), gets the goods examined and pays the import duty; the goods are then released.

learn.hook: International trade runs on paper (or PDFs): one document orders, another guarantees payment, another proves the goods are on the ship. Mix them up and the cargo gets stuck.
points: Indent: an order placed by the importer with the exporter for supply of goods. Proforma invoice: a quotation giving details of quality, grade, size, weight, price and terms.

Letter of credit (LC): a guarantee by the importer's bank that it will honour payment up to a certain amount on presentation of specified documents. Certificate of origin: shows the country of manufacture.
Shipping order: issued by the shipping company to the ship's captain to receive the specified goods on board. Shipping bill: the main document for customs permission to export.

Mate's receipt: issued by the captain after the cargo is loaded. Bill of lading: issued by the shipping company accepting goods for carriage by sea; a document of title. Airway bill: the equivalent document for goods sent by air.

Bill of exchange: a written instrument in which the exporter (drawer) orders the importer (drawee) to pay a certain sum to a specified person. Sight draft: payable on presentation (documents released against payment). Usance draft: payable after a specified period (documents released against acceptance).

learn.hook: Which body sets rules so that 160-plus countries can trade without endless trade wars? The World Trade Organization, headquartered in Geneva.
points: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), signed in 1947 and effective from 1948, governed world trade for decades. The Uruguay Round of negotiations led to the creation of the World Trade Organization (WTO), which came into being on 1 January 1995 as the successor to GATT.

The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. India is a founder member. Unlike GATT, the WTO is a permanent organisation with a legal status, and it covers trade in goods, services and intellectual property.

Objectives: to raise standards of living; to ensure full employment and growth in real income and effective demand; to expand production and trade in goods and services; to ensure optimal use of the world's resources; to protect the environment and promote sustainable development; to help developing countries get a fair share of growth in world trade; and to reduce tariffs and other trade barriers and eliminate discrimination.
Note: the complexities of international business, export promotion incentives and support organisations, and export processing zones were removed in rationalisation and are not covered here.

revise.summary: The WTO, successor to GATT, came into being on 1 January 1995 after the Uruguay Round and is based in Geneva. It is a permanent body covering goods, services and IP, aiming to expand trade, raise living standards and reduce trade barriers.
focus: Dates: GATT 1947/1948, WTO 1 January 1995
How the WTO differs from GATT
Objectives of the WTO
remember: WTO: 1 January 1995, Geneva, successor to GATT
GATT: signed 1947, effective 1948
India is a founder member
traps: Don't say the WTO was set up in 1948; that was GATT
The WTO's headquarters is Geneva, not New York
The WTO aims to reduce, not raise, tariffs
